Every screen has things pushing in from: The status bar, the home indicator, the keyboard, and your own headers and tab bars.
Harbor gives each one a place, so your content stops doing inset arithmetic.
It starts with the root. Mount it once, above your navigator, and every frame sits on it.
The system edges are what the platform takes: the status bar, the home indicator, a notch.
An overlay bar is a header your content scrolls under.
Like a pier, built out over the water.
Boats pass beneath a pier, the way your rows slide under the header.
A solid bar is a tab bar your content stops at.
Like a quay, a stone wall on the shore.
The tug pulls up to the quay wall, and the list comes to rest right above the tab bar.
An edge effect is what content does under a bar, like the ripples a boat leaves behind.
Rows fade as they slide under the header, then rest past the fade.
Clear is a safe area that also knows about the bars and the keyboard.
A form or a fixed button keeps clear of the bars, the system edges and the keyboard.
Row insets are the page margin, kept by the rows that ask for it.
The list runs to the edge of the screen, so a carousel inside it can too.
The scroll view is your list, and like a channel, it runs under the bars.
It comes to rest clear of them at both ends.
A sliver bar is a header inside the list. It pins at the face of the bars, and the next one stacks below it.
A sticky pill rides with its row, then holds below the bars until the row scrolls away.
Some content ignores the bars: a background, a map, a hero image.
It runs under the header, edge to edge, and asks the room how far the bars reach.
Then there is the keyboard, and each bar takes a stance.
When it comes in, a bar that stays is covered, like a jetty on pilings. That's your tab bar.
A bar that rides comes up with it, like a floating dock. That's your composer, sitting right on top of the keyboard.
A bar that reserves holds the keyboard's space, like a dry dock.
The keyboard goes out and a panel takes its place. When it comes back, nothing moves.
Content can ask a bar to hide: to go dark, or to withdraw and give back its space.
An attached bar is added from deep inside the page, like an unsaved changes bar.
A float sits in the room: a floating button, a speech bubble by its anchor.
A float with a barrier is modal. Tap beside it, or go back, and it closes.
A popover opens from anywhere: a menu from a list row flips above it when there is no room.
Show a toast, and it goes to the page on top, clear of the bars, and screen readers announce it.
A sheet is a page of its own, with its own header and a footer that rides the keyboard.
It stops short of the status bar, and its footer clears the home indicator once.
A sheet that covers the page tells the page how much is covered, so the page keeps clear of it.
A dialog can keep to the room of the page that opened it.
Keep visible does what it says: a focused field is brought back above the keyboard.
The inspector shows every bar's space, each frame's room, and the keyboard, as you work.
Trials test it all in widget tests, on phones and foldables, with the keyboard up.
Every edge is claimed once, and your content gets the room.
